### Packages and Data

```{r load-packages, message=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

```

## Data set: college recent grads

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(fivethirtyeight)
college_grad_df <- college_recent_grads
# First look at your data set
glimpse(college_grad_df)
```


# Exercise 1: Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r}

college_grad_df %>% ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x= median), fill = "plum")

college_grad_df %>% ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x= median), fill = "palevioletred", binwidth = 2500)


college_grad_df %>%
  count(major_category, sort = TRUE)

```

_With a bandwidth of 2500, the histogram provides greater detail as the specified bandwidth is smaller than the standard, resulting in more bars. Regardless, the model is right leaning, leading to a positive skew, the count peaking/concentrated around a median of 3.5e+04. It also seems like there is a potential outlier around 1.1e+05_


# Exercise 2: Exploring relationship

```{r}
college_grad_df %>% drop_na(sharewomen, median) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sharewomen, y= median)) +
  geom_point(colour = "plum") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "palevioletred") 


coef(lm(median ~ sharewomen, data = college_grad_df))

```

_From the scatter plot, there is a distinct negative correlation between a higher share of women and majors with lower median earnings, the formula of the line of best fit being: y = 56100 - 30700x, where y is median and x is sharewomen. Additionally, the negative gradient of -30700 indicates that for every 1 unit increase in the proportion of women, the predicted median earnings decrease by roughly $30,700._

# Exercise 3: Fit and interpret a numerical predictor

```{r}

share_fit = linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(median ~ sharewomen, data = college_grad_df)

tidy(share_fit)

glance(share_fit)

share_fit_aug = augment(share_fit$fit)

share_fit_aug %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray", lty = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals")



```

_median = 56100 - 30700 sharewomen, is the formula of the fitted model. The negative gradient of -30700 indicates that for every 1 unit increase in the proportion of women, the predicted median earnings decrease by roughly $30,700 - just like the initial visualisation._

_Doesn't seem like there is a distinct trend or pattern, insinuating that a linear model may be suitable to model the data, however one could argue that the scatter plots fan out slightly at the end as the fitted values increase._

# Exercise 4: Consider a categorical variable instead 

```{r}

college_grad_df = college_grad_df %>% mutate(
  engineering = case_when(
    str_detect(major, regex("engineering", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Engineering",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )
)

share_fit2 = linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(median ~ engineering, data = college_grad_df)

tidy(share_fit2)

glance(share_fit2)

share_fit2_aug = augment(share_fit2$fit)

share_fit2_aug %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray", lty = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals")

levels(as.factor(college_grad_df$engineering))


```

_The baseline category is Engineering. The intercept of 58,388.46 represents the average median earnings of Engineering majors, approximately $58,388.46. The slope of -21,462.61 indicates that Other majors have average median earnings approximately $21,462.61 lower than Engineering majors, giving them predicted average median earnings of $36,925.85._

## Data set: Beauty in the classroom

```{r read-data}
evals<-read.csv("data/evals.csv", row.names=1)
```


# Exercise 1: Exploratory Data Analysis

1.  Visualize the distribution of `score` in the dataframe `evals`.

```{r viz-score}

evals %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "plum") 

evals %>%
  summarise(
    mean = mean(score, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(score, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(score, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(score, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(score, na.rm = TRUE)
  )



```

_Model is left leaning, hence resulting in a negative skew showing that students generally rate courses higher._

2.  Visualize and describe the relationship between `score` and `bty_avg` using `geom_point()` to represent the data. 

```{r scatterplot}

evals %>% drop_na(score, bty_avg) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bty_avg, y= score)) +
  geom_point(colour = "plum") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "palevioletred") 

evals %>% drop_na(score, bty_avg) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bty_avg, y= score)) +
  geom_jitter(colour = "mediumpurple") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "cornflowerblue") 

```

_Jitter adds small amount of noise. Multiple observations share identical bty_avg and score values. These observations overlap, making them appear as a single point. This creates the misleading impression that there are fewer observations in certain regions than there actually are. Jitter makes the density and frequency of observations easier to see._
